content: In the documentation for Inductive types, specifically in Theorem Proving For Lean, various constants such as rec, brecOn, noConfusion and a few others are said to be automatically generated for any inductive type. Could I know the comprehensive list of these constants which Lean automatically generates for inductive types?

here's a small example

import Mathlib.Util.WhatsNew

/--
info: def Foo._sizeOf_inst : SizeOf Foo :=
{ sizeOf := fun m => m._sizeOf_1 }

protected def Foo.ctorIdx : Foo → Nat :=
fun x => Foo.casesOn x (fun n => 0) (fun foo => 1) fun n children => 2

theorem Foo.branch.inj : ∀ {n : Nat} {children : Fin n → Foo} {n_1 : Nat} {children_1 : Fin n_1 → Foo},
  Foo.branch n children = Foo.branch n_1 children_1 → n = n_1 ∧ children ≍ children_1 :=
fun {n} {children} {n_1} {children_1} x => Foo.branch.noConfusion x fun n_eq children_eq => ⟨n_eq, children_eq⟩

protected def Foo.noConfusionType.{u} : Sort u → Foo → Foo → Sort u :=
fun P t t' =>
  Foo.casesOn t (fun n => if h : t'.ctorIdx = 0 then Foo.nat.elim t' h fun n_1 => (n = n_1 → P) → P else P)
    (fun foo => if h : t'.ctorIdx = 1 then Foo.wrap.elim t' h fun foo_1 => (foo = foo_1 → P) → P else P)
    fun n children =>
    if h : t'.ctorIdx = 2 then Foo.branch.elim t' h fun n_1 children_1 => (n = n_1 → children ≍ children_1 → P) → P
    else P

def Foo.branch.noConfusion.{u} : {P : Sort u} →
  {n : Nat} →
    {children : Fin n → Foo} →
      {n' : Nat} →
        {children' : Fin n' → Foo} →
          Foo.branch n children = Foo.branch n' children' → (n = n' → children ≍ children' → P) → P :=
fun {P} {n} {children} {n'} {children'} eq k => id (Foo.noConfusion eq k)

protected def Foo.ctorElim.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} →
  (ctorIdx : Nat) → (t : Foo) → ctorIdx = t.ctorIdx → Foo.ctorElimType ctorIdx → motive t :=
fun {motive} ctorIdx t h k =>
  Foo.casesOn (motive := fun t => ctorIdx = t.ctorIdx → motive t) t (fun n h => (h ▸ k).down n)
    (fun foo h => (h ▸ k).down foo) (fun n children h => (h ▸ k).down n children) h

recursor Foo.rec.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} →
  ((n : Nat) → motive (Foo.nat n)) →
    ((foo : Foo) → motive foo → motive foo.wrap) →
      ((n : Nat) → (children : Fin n → Foo) → ((a : Fin n) → motive (children a)) → motive (Foo.branch n children)) →
        (t : Foo) → motive t

def Foo._sizeOf_1 : Foo → Nat :=
fun t => Foo.rec (fun n => 1 + sizeOf n) (fun foo foo_ih => 1 + foo_ih) (fun n children children_ih => 1 + sizeOf n) t

constructor Foo.branch : (n : Nat) → (Fin n → Foo) → Foo

protected def Foo.noConfusion.{u} : {P : Sort u} → {t t' : Foo} → t = t' → Foo.noConfusionType P t t' :=
fun {P} {t t'} eq => eq ▸ Foo.casesOn t (fun n k => k ⋯) (fun foo k => k ⋯) fun n children k => k ⋯ ⋯

def Foo.wrap.noConfusion.{u} : {P : Sort u} → {foo foo' : Foo} → foo.wrap = foo'.wrap → (foo = foo' → P) → P :=
fun {P} {foo foo'} eq k => id (Foo.noConfusion eq k)

def Foo.nat.noConfusion.{u} : {P : Sort u} → {n n' : Nat} → Foo.nat n = Foo.nat n' → (n = n' → P) → P :=
fun {P} {n n'} eq k => id (Foo.noConfusion eq k)

protected def Foo.recOn.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} →
  (t : Foo) →
    ((n : Nat) → motive (Foo.nat n)) →
      ((foo : Foo) → motive foo → motive foo.wrap) →
        ((n : Nat) → (children : Fin n → Foo) → ((a : Fin n) → motive (children a)) → motive (Foo.branch n children)) →
          motive t :=
fun {motive} t nat wrap branch => Foo.rec nat wrap branch t

theorem Foo.wrap.inj : ∀ {foo foo_1 : Foo}, foo.wrap = foo_1.wrap → foo = foo_1 :=
fun {foo foo_1} x => Foo.wrap.noConfusion x fun foo_eq => foo_eq

theorem Foo.nat.inj : ∀ {n n_1 : Nat}, Foo.nat n = Foo.nat n_1 → n = n_1 :=
fun {n n_1} x => Foo.nat.noConfusion x fun n_eq => n_eq

constructor Foo.wrap : Foo → Foo

constructor Foo.nat : Nat → Foo

inductive Foo : Type
constructors:
Foo.nat : Nat → Foo
Foo.wrap : Foo → Foo
Foo.branch : (n : Nat) → (Fin n → Foo) → Foo

theorem Foo.wrap.sizeOf_spec : ∀ (foo : Foo), sizeOf foo.wrap = 1 + sizeOf foo :=
fun foo => Eq.refl (1 + sizeOf foo)

theorem Foo.nat.sizeOf_spec : ∀ (n : Nat), sizeOf (Foo.nat n) = 1 + sizeOf n :=
fun n => Eq.refl (1 + sizeOf n)

protected def Foo.brecOn.go.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} →
  (t : Foo) → ((t : Foo) → Foo.below t → motive t) → motive t ×' Foo.below t :=
fun {motive} t F_1 =>
  Foo.rec (fun n => ⟨F_1 (Foo.nat n) PUnit.unit, PUnit.unit⟩) (fun foo foo_ih => ⟨F_1 foo.wrap foo_ih, foo_ih⟩)
    (fun n children children_ih => ⟨F_1 (Foo.branch n children) children_ih, children_ih⟩) t

theorem Foo.wrap.injEq : ∀ (foo foo_1 : Foo), (foo.wrap = foo_1.wrap) = (foo = foo_1) :=
fun foo foo_1 => Eq.propIntro Foo.wrap.inj (Eq.ndrec (Eq.refl foo.wrap))

theorem Foo.nat.injEq : ∀ (n n_1 : Nat), (Foo.nat n = Foo.nat n_1) = (n = n_1) :=
fun n n_1 => Eq.propIntro Foo.nat.inj (Eq.ndrec (Eq.refl (Foo.nat n)))

protected def Foo.nat.elim.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} →
  (t : Foo) → t.ctorIdx = 0 → ((n : Nat) → motive (Foo.nat n)) → motive t :=
fun {motive} t h nat => Foo.ctorElim 0 t ⋯ { down := nat }

protected def Foo.wrap.elim.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} →
  (t : Foo) → t.ctorIdx = 1 → ((foo : Foo) → motive foo.wrap) → motive t :=
fun {motive} t h wrap => Foo.ctorElim 1 t ⋯ { down := wrap }

protected def Foo.brecOn.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} → (t : Foo) → ((t : Foo) → Foo.below t → motive t) → motive t :=
fun {motive} t F_1 => (Foo.brecOn.go t F_1).1

protected def Foo.below.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} → Foo → Sort (max 1 u) :=
fun {motive} t =>
  Foo.rec (fun n => PUnit) (fun foo foo_ih => motive foo ×' foo_ih)
    (fun n children children_ih => (a : Fin n) → motive (children a) ×' children_ih a) t

protected theorem Foo.brecOn.eq.{u} : ∀ {motive : Foo → Sort u} (t : Foo) (F_1 : (t : Foo) → Foo.below t → motive t),
  Foo.brecOn t F_1 = F_1 t (Foo.brecOn.go t F_1).2 :=
fun {motive} t F_1 =>
  Foo.casesOn t (fun n => Eq.refl (Foo.brecOn (Foo.nat n) F_1)) (fun foo => Eq.refl (Foo.brecOn foo.wrap F_1))
    fun n children => Eq.refl (Foo.brecOn (Foo.branch n children) F_1)

protected def Foo.ctorElimType.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} → Nat → Sort (max 1 u) :=
fun {motive} ctorIdx =>
  bif ctorIdx.ble 0 then PULift ((n : Nat) → motive (Foo.nat n))
  else
    bif ctorIdx.ble 1 then PULift ((foo : Foo) → motive foo.wrap)
    else PULift ((n : Nat) → (children : Fin n → Foo) → motive (Foo.branch n children))

theorem Foo.branch.injEq : ∀ (n : Nat) (children : Fin n → Foo) (n_1 : Nat) (children_1 : Fin n_1 → Foo),
  (Foo.branch n children = Foo.branch n_1 children_1) = (n = n_1 ∧ children ≍ children_1) :=
fun n children n_1 children_1 =>
  Eq.propIntro Foo.branch.inj
    (Lean.injEq_helper fun a =>
      Eq.ndrec (motive := fun n_2 =>
        ∀ (children_2 : Fin n_2 → Foo), children ≍ children_2 → Foo.branch n children = Foo.branch n_2 children_2)
        (fun children_2 => HEq.homo_ndrec (Eq.refl (Foo.branch n children))) a children_1)

protected def Foo.branch.elim.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} →
  (t : Foo) → t.ctorIdx = 2 → ((n : Nat) → (children : Fin n → Foo) → motive (Foo.branch n children)) → motive t :=
fun {motive} t h branch => Foo.ctorElim 2 t ⋯ { down := branch }

def Foo.casesOn.{u} : {motive : Foo → Sort u} →
  (t : Foo) →
    ((n : Nat) → motive (Foo.nat n)) →
      ((foo : Foo) → motive foo.wrap) →
        ((n : Nat) → (children : Fin n → Foo) → motive (Foo.branch n children)) → motive t :=
fun {motive} t nat wrap branch =>
  Foo.rec (fun n => nat n) (fun foo foo_ih => wrap foo) (fun n children children_ih => branch n children) t

theorem Foo.branch.sizeOf_spec : ∀ (n : Nat) (children : Fin n → Foo), sizeOf (Foo.branch n children) = 1 + sizeOf n :=
fun n children => Eq.refl (1 + sizeOf n)

-- Lean.auxRecExt extension: 8 new entries

-- _private.Lean.AuxRecursor.0.Lean.sparseCasesOnExt extension: 3 new entries

-- Lean.noConfusionExt extension: 4 new entries

-- Lean.declRangeExt extension: 4 new entries

-- Lean.protectedExt extension: 13 new entries

-- _private.Lean.Namespace.0.Lean.namespacesExt extension: 5 new entries

-- reducibilityCore extension: 16 new entries

-- Lean.Meta.instanceExtension extension: 1 new entries

-- Lean.IR.declMapExt extension: 11 new entries

-- _private.Lean.Compiler.LCNF.MonoTypes.0.Lean.Compiler.LCNF.trivialStructureInfoExt extension: 1 new entries

-- Lean.Compiler.LCNF.monoTypeExt extension: 4 new entries

-- Lean.Compiler.LCNF.baseExt extension: 5 new entries

-- Lean.Compiler.LCNF.monoExt extension: 9 new entries

-- Lean.Compiler.LCNF.impureSigExt extension: 11 new entries

-- _private.Lean.Compiler.LCNF.ToImpureType.0.Lean.Compiler.LCNF.impureTypeExt extension: 1 new entries

-- _private.Lean.Compiler.LCNF.ToImpureType.0.Lean.Compiler.LCNF.impureTrivialStructureInfoExt extension: 1 new entries

-- _private.Lean.Compiler.LCNF.ToImpureType.0.Lean.Compiler.LCNF.ctorLayoutExt extension: 3 new entries

-- Lean.Compiler.LCNF.UnreachableBranches.functionSummariesExt extension: 9 new entries

-- Lean.Meta.simpExtension extension: 6 new entries

-- Lean.Meta.completionBlackListExt extension: 7 new entries

-- Lean.Elab.Term.elabAsElim extension: 3 new entries

-- Lean.Meta.Grind.grindExt extension: 3 new entries
-/
#guard_msgs in
whatsnew in
inductive Foo where
  | nat (n : Nat) : Foo
  | wrap (foo : Foo) : Foo
  | branch (n : Nat) (children : Fin n → Foo) : Foo
Well, the example is small, the definitions it generates aren't!

Thanks! I was also curious to know if strict positivity is the necessary and sufficient condition to define an inductive type.
Also, will Lean automatically show that my inductive type defines a WellFounded relation, as result of which I can use the WellFounded.fix induction principle?

Pranav cs22b015 said:

Thanks! I was also curious to know if strict positivity is the necessary and sufficient condition to define an inductive type.

Necessary, also practically sufficient but there are a couple of other conditions too regarding universe sizes, parameter uniformity.

Also, will Lean automatically show that my inductive type defines a WellFounded relation, as result of which I can use the WellFounded.fix induction principle?

Yes, it generates docs#SizeOf, which has docs#sizeOfWFRel. Is there any reason you're not using regular induction?

Thanks!
Theorem Proving in Lean says

To handle structural recursion, the equation compiler uses course-of-values recursion, using constants below and brecOn that are automatically generated with each inductively defined type.

Nat.brecOn.{u} {motive : Nat → Sort u} (t : Nat) (F_1 : (t : Nat) → Nat.below t → motive t) : motive t

Now, under the WellFounded recursion section, the Fix function is as follows -

noncomputable
def f {α : Sort u}
    (r : α → α → Prop)
    (h : WellFounded r)
    (C : α → Sort v)
    (F : (x : α) → ((y : α) → r y x → C y) → C x) :
    (x : α) → C x :=
WellFounded.fix h F

What is the exact difference between these kinds of induction? The idea seems similar, both use the principle of strong induction in mathematical terms

Another side question I had was that certain types like Bool don't have below or brecOn, so which kind of inductive types support these postulates?

In my understanding any inductive type with a recursive constructor gets below & brecOn since Bool has none these are omitted . For example 

inductive color where
| red : color
| blue : color
| green : color

#check color.rec
#check color.below --error

As brecOn is useful when a value contains a smaller value of same type since Bool has no such constructors and therefore its below would be empty and brecOn adds nothing over the rec in such case.

From a type theory perspective, the only thing you get "for free" from the theory is the recursor, i.e. *.rec, as well as some definitional reduction rules. The reduction rules are nameless since they're part of the foundational theory of Lean, they are why you can prove 1 + 2 = 3 := by rfl. All the other auxiliary eliminators such as *.below, *.brecOn, *.recOn, .noConfusion etc etc etc are theorems derived from the eliminator and reduction rules, which Lean's inductive type elaborator helpfully automatically proves for you when you add an inductive type. Specifically *.rec is not generated by Lean, it's part of the theory, it's a primitive.

Note that you don't need WellFounded.fix to recurse on an inductive type. You have the eliminator *.rec. You can try implementing some simple recursive function directly as an exercise if you want: def map (xs : List A) (f : A -> B) : List B := List.rec (motive := ...) sorry sorry xs. Actually, there is the inductive type Acc with its own eliminator Acc.rec, from which WellFounded.fix is derived.

(I hope I'm not re-explaining something that's obvious to you :P.)
If you wanted to, you could ignore .below, .brecOn, etc and you theoretically wouldn't lose any expressive power. You can define/prove those yourself. But if you get rid of .rec, you're screwed.

Thanks a lot, this made things a lot clearer. I'm still curious about how Lean decides which mode of recursion to use - structural or well-founded.
For example, the function

def search {α} (f : Nat → Option α) (start : Nat) (to : Nat) : Option α :=
  match f start with
  | .some x => .some x
  | .none =>
    if start < to then
      search f (start + 1) to
    else
      .none

is shown to terminate using WellFounded.fix automatically. This was earlier an example of having to manually specifiy termination_by manually (in https://web.archive.org/web/20250618125453/https://lean-lang.org/blog/2024-1-11-recursive-definitions-in-lean/).
